```{r}
#| label: supp-rt-summaries

# Per-run and per-cell response-time summaries used in the sections below.
# Rebuilt here rather than inherited: the earlier versions lived in
# mental_rotation.qmd (outside this paper's include chain) and referred to
# columns that no longer exist.
# mirrors the rt-angle-data chunk in _02_angle_sensitivity.qmd; rebuilt here so
# the supplementary renders without refitting the main models.
deg <- 40 # angle unit size
yrs <- 2  # age unit size

# filter to non-CAT, add age group, stimulus, angle
mrot_lme_data <- mrot_rt_trial |>
  filter(#!adaptive,            # exclude CAT runs
         correct == 1,         # exclude incorrect responses
         trial_number != 1) |> # exclude each run's first trial
  mutate(
    item_group = factor(item_group),
    stimulus   = factor(stimulus),
    site_label = factor(site_label),
    angle_sc   = (angle - mean(angle)) / deg, # scale to 1 unit = 40
    adaptive   = factor(adaptive), 
    age_sc     = (age - mean(age)) / yrs, # scale to 2 units = sd
    task       = "mrot"  # constant; slope_preds uses it for the overall effect
  ) |>
  select(site_label, user_id, run_id,  matches("age"), trial_number,
         item_group, stimulus, angle, angle_sc, rt_s, log_rt, adaptive, task)

# effects code all factors

# effects code all factors
contrasts(mrot_lme_data$site_label) <- contr.sum(levels(mrot_lme_data$site_label))
contrasts(mrot_lme_data$item_group) <- contr.sum(levels(mrot_lme_data$item_group))
contrasts(mrot_lme_data$stimulus) <- contr.sum(levels(mrot_lme_data$stimulus))

supp_rt_runs <- mrot_rt_trial |>
  filter(correct == 1, trial_number != 1, is.finite(log_rt)) |>
  summarise(rt_med = median(log_rt, na.rm = TRUE),
            .by = c(site_label, user_id, run_id, age, stimulus, item_group, angle)) |>
  mutate(age_group = cut(age, breaks = age_breaks, include.lowest = TRUE, right = FALSE)) |>
  drop_na(age_group)   # age_group needed: the figure facets site_label ~ age_group

supp_rt_cells <- supp_rt_runs |>
  summarise(y = mean(rt_med, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd = sd(rt_med, na.rm = TRUE),
            n = n(),
            .by = c(site_label, stimulus, item_group, angle, age_group)) |>
  mutate(se = sd / sqrt(pmax(n, 1)), lwr = y - 1.96 * se, upr = y + 1.96 * se)
```

```{r coef-scatter}
# load configural parameters
mrot_configural <- mrot_coefs |>
  filter(task == "mrot",
         itemtype == "2pl",
         invariance == "configural",
         model_set == "multigroup_dataset") |>
  mutate(site_label = group |>
           recode_values(from = site_labels, to = names(site_labels))) |>
  select(item, site_label, difficulty, discrimination = a1)

# pivot wide
mrot_wide_d <- mrot_configural |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = site_label, values_from = c(difficulty, discrimination)) |>
  separate_wider_delim(item, delim = "_",
                       names = c("task", "group", "stimulus", "angle")) |>
  mutate(angle = as.integer(angle),
         item_label = glue("{stimulus} {angle}°"))

param_ranges <- list(
  "difficulty" = range(mrot_configural$difficulty),
  "discrimination" = range(mrot_configural$discrimination)
)
coef_scatter <- function(param, x_site, y_site) {
  x_var <- paste(param, x_site, sep = "_")
  y_var <- paste(param, y_site, sep = "_")
  x_lab <- glue("{str_to_sentence(param)} ({x_site})")
  y_lab <- glue("{str_to_sentence(param)} ({y_site})")
  ggplot(mrot_wide_d, aes(x = .data[[x_var]], y = .data[[y_var]])) +
    coord_equal(xlim = param_ranges[[param]], ylim = param_ranges[[param]]) +
    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1,
                linetype = "dashed", colour = pal$grey) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = stimulus), size = 2.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_text_repel(aes(label = item_label), size = 2.8, family = .font,
                    max.overlaps = Inf, box.padding = 0.5, point.padding = 0.3) +
    .scale_colour_stimulus(guide = "none") +
    labs(x = x_lab, y = y_lab)
}

sites <- names(site_labels)
site_pairs <- expand_grid(s1 = 1:4, s2 = 1:4) |>
  filter(s2 > s1) |>
  mutate(s1 = sites[s1], s2 = sites[s2])
```

\clearpage
## Prediction weighting: observed data versus a balanced grid

Angle slopes in the main text are average marginal effects computed over the administered trials. They therefore estimate the angle effect for the average trial in this study. A balanced grid instead estimates the effect for a hypothetical population with equal numbers of observations in each site × age × item-type cell.

Cell sizes are substantially unbalanced (Table S2): the largest contains more than 20 times as many trials as the smallest. The sparsest cells all contain 3D items, with the two sparsest comprising 3D items administered to the youngest children. Observed-data averaging weights each cell in proportion to its trial count, whereas a balanced grid weights all cells equally. Thus, compared with observed-data averaging, a balanced grid gives the sparsest cell approximately eight times as much weight and the largest approximately one third as much. Equal weighting also shifts the age composition toward younger children more strongly for 3D than for 2D items. Because the multiplicative angle slope increases with age, this shift affects the 3D estimate more than the 2D estimate. Table S3 reports the angle slopes under both weighting schemes.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cell-weights
#| tbl-cap: "Trials and children per cell, with the weight each cell receives under observed-data averaging and under a balanced grid. Inflation is the ratio of the balanced-grid weight to the observed weight: values above 1 indicate cells whose influence a balanced grid increases, values below 1 cells whose influence it reduces."

cell_weights <- mrot_lme_data |>
  summarise(trials = n(), children = n_distinct(user_id),
            .by = c(site_label, age_group, item_group)) |>
  mutate(obs_wt = 100 * trials / sum(trials),
         grid_wt = 100 / n(),
         inflation = grid_wt / obs_wt) |>
  arrange(site_label, age_group, item_group) |>
  mutate(item_group = str_to_upper(item_group),
         age_group = as.character(age_group) |>
           str_replace_all(c("\\[" = "", "\\]" = "", "\\)" = "", "," = "--")),
         across(c(obs_wt, grid_wt), \(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)),
         inflation = sprintf("%.2f", inflation))

cell_tbl <- knitr::kable(
  cell_weights,
  col.names = c("Site", "Age group", "Item type", "Trials", "Children",
                "Observed wt. (%)", "Grid wt. (%)", "Inflation"),
  booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = c("l", "l", "l", rep("r", 5))
)

# Shrink only for LaTeX: kable_styling emits HTML, which Quarto rejects when
# rendering to docx. Without it the wide site labels wrap in the PDF.
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  cell_tbl <- kableExtra::kable_styling(cell_tbl, latex_options = "HOLD_position",
                                        font_size = 9)
}
cell_tbl
```

\clearpage
## Angle slopes under each weighting scheme

```{r}
#| label: supp-weight-models
#| cache: true

# Refit the main-text angle model here: marginal effects over a balanced grid
# require the fitted model object, which the summaries above do not carry.
full_mod_supp <- lmer(log_rt ~ angle_sc * stimulus * site_label * age_sc +
                        trial_number * stimulus +
                        adaptive * stimulus +
                        (1 + angle_sc | user_id),
                      data = mrot_lme_data, REML = FALSE,
                      control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

# Balanced grid, built as in _02_angle_sensitivity.qmd
stim_map_supp <- mrot_lme_data |> distinct(angle, angle_sc, item_group, stimulus)
angle_levels_supp <- mrot_lme_data |> distinct(angle) |> arrange(angle)
age_seq_supp <- seq(min(mrot_lme_data$age_sc), max(mrot_lme_data$age_sc), length.out = 100)

pred_grid_supp <- datagrid(angle_sc = unique, stimulus = unique, site_label = unique,
                           age_sc = age_seq_supp, trial_number = mean, adaptive = unique,
                           newdata = mrot_lme_data) |>
  select(rowid, angle_sc, stimulus, site_label, age_sc, adaptive, trial_number) |>
  mutate(age = age_sc * sd(mrot_lme_data$age) + mean(mrot_lme_data$age),
         age = map_dbl(age, \(a) max(a, min(mrot_lme_data$age))),
         age_group = cut(age, breaks = age_breaks, include.lowest = FALSE, right = FALSE),
         task = "mrot") |>
  inner_join(stim_map_supp, by = c("angle_sc", "stimulus")) |>
  left_join(mrot_lme_data |> distinct(angle, angle_sc), by = c("angle", "angle_sc"))

slopes_by <- function(newdata, pred) {
  slopes(full_mod_supp, newdata = newdata, re.form = NA,
         variables = "angle_sc", by = pred) |>
    as_tibble() |> rename(value = !!pred) |>
    transmute(predictor = pred, value = as.character(value), estimate)
}

weight_compare <- map(c("task", "item_group", "site_label", "age_group"), \(pred) {
  left_join(slopes_by(mrot_lme_data, pred) |> rename(observed = estimate),
            slopes_by(pred_grid_supp, pred) |> rename(grid = estimate),
            by = c("predictor", "value"))
}) |> list_rbind() |> filter(!is.na(value), value != "NA")

# Quantities quoted in the text, so they track the fitted model.
at_mean_age <- mrot_lme_data |> mutate(age_sc = 0)

item_slopes <- \(nd) slopes(full_mod_supp, newdata = nd, re.form = NA,
                           variables = "angle_sc", by = "item_group") |> as_tibble()
item_contrast <- \(nd) slopes(full_mod_supp, newdata = nd, re.form = NA,
                             variables = "angle_sc", by = "item_group",
                             hypothesis = "b2 - b1 = 0") |> as_tibble()

obs_item   <- item_slopes(mrot_lme_data)
grid_item  <- item_slopes(pred_grid_supp)
fixed_item <- item_slopes(at_mean_age)

sl  <- \(tbl, g) sprintf("%.3f", tbl$estimate[tbl$item_group == g])
age_share_pct <- round(100 * abs(item_contrast(at_mean_age)$estimate) /
                         abs(item_contrast(pred_grid_supp)$estimate))
fixed_ctr <- item_contrast(at_mean_age)

youngest <- levels(mrot_lme_data$age_group)[1]
young_row <- weight_compare |> filter(predictor == "age_group", value == youngest)
stopifnot(nrow(young_row) == 1)
```

The main text reports slopes averaged over the observed trials, a choice made after computing both sets of estimates. A balanced grid most strongly upweights cells containing 3D items administered to the youngest children, where the model's four-way interaction between angle, stimulus type, site, and age is least well identified; the sparsest cell contains 183 trials from 40 children. The balanced-grid 3D estimate therefore relies substantially on model-based predictions in cells with limited supporting data. Holding age at the sample mean rather than averaging over the observed age distribution accounts for approximately `r age_share_pct`% of the difference between schemes (2D = `r sl(fixed_item, "2d")`, 3D = `r sl(fixed_item, "3d")`; contrast = `r sprintf("%.3f", fixed_ctr$estimate)`, *p* `r fmt_p(fixed_ctr$p.value)`); the remainder reflects equal weighting of the sparse cells.



```{r}
#| label: tbl-weight-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Marginal angle slopes from the same fitted model, averaged over the observed trials and over a balanced grid of cells. Slopes are on the log response time scale, so a value of 0.14 corresponds to approximately 15% longer response times per 40° of rotation. The final column is the grid estimate minus the observed estimate."

weight_compare |>
  mutate(
    predictor = recode(predictor, task = "Overall", item_group = "Item type",
                       site_label = "Site", age_group = "Age group"),
    value = value |>
      str_replace_all(c("^mrot$" = "All trials", "^2d$" = "2D", "^3d$" = "3D",
                        "\\[" = "", "\\]" = "", "\\)" = "", "," = "--")),
    across(c(observed, grid), \(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)),
    diff = sprintf("%+.3f", as.numeric(grid) - as.numeric(observed))
  ) |>
  select(predictor, value, observed, grid, diff) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("", "Level", "Observed trials", "Balanced grid", "Difference"),
    booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r")
  )
```

\clearpage
## Response time scale: multiplicative versus additive

Response times are modelled on a log scale throughout, so the angle slopes reported in the main text describe a multiplicative cost — a constant percentage increase per 40° of rotation. The classic chronometric result [@shepard1971mental] is instead additive: a constant increment in milliseconds per degree, implying a constant rate of rotation. This section reports the angle effect under both specifications and the basis for modelling on the log scale.

@tbl-scale-compare gives the angle slope from the model reported in the main text and from the same specification fitted to untransformed response times. The two agree on direction and, with one exception, on ordering: response time rises with angle overall, within each stimulus type and at every site, and the age gradient is monotonic under both. The exception is that uniandes-co-rural and western-ca exchange rank. The two stimulus types illustrate what the choice of scale does: their multiplicative costs are almost identical, whereas their additive costs differ by a factor of two. This is a single fact expressed two ways, since an equal multiplicative cost applied to a baseline that is 2.28 times higher yields twice the absolute cost. The additive estimates are also directly comparable with the chronometric literature, which reports rotation rate in milliseconds per degree.

```{r}
#| label: supp-scale-models
#| cache: true

# The same specification fitted to untransformed RT, for comparison.
m_raw_supp <- lmer(rt_s ~ angle_sc * stimulus * site_label * age_sc +
                     trial_number * stimulus + adaptive * stimulus +
                     (1 + angle_sc | user_id),
                   data = mrot_lme_data, REML = FALSE,
                   control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

scale_rows <- function(mod, pred, scale) {
  slopes(mod, newdata = mrot_lme_data, re.form = NA,
         variables = "angle_sc", by = pred) |>
    as_tibble() |> rename(value = !!pred) |>
    transmute(predictor = pred, value = as.character(value), scale, estimate)
}
preds <- c("task", "item_group", "site_label", "age_group")
scale_compare <- bind_rows(
  map(preds, \(p) scale_rows(full_mod_supp, p, "log")) |> list_rbind(),
  map(preds, \(p) scale_rows(m_raw_supp,    p, "raw")) |> list_rbind()
) |>
  mutate(shown = if_else(scale == "log",
                         sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (exp(estimate) - 1)),
                         sprintf("%.1f", 1000 * estimate / 40))) |>
  select(-estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = scale, values_from = shown)

# Box-Cox needs an lm, so lambda is estimated from a fixed-effects simplification.
bc <- MASS::boxcox(lm(rt_s ~ angle_sc * stimulus + site_label + age_sc,
                      data = mrot_lme_data),
                   lambda = seq(-0.4, 0.6, 0.01), plotit = FALSE)
bc_lambda <- bc$x[which.max(bc$y)]
bc_ci <- range(bc$x[bc$y > max(bc$y) - qchisq(.95, 1) / 2])

# Likelihoods on different response scales are not comparable without the
# Jacobian: f_Y(y) = f_Z(log y) / y, so subtract sum(log y) to express the
# log-scale fit on the seconds scale.
aic_log_on_raw <- -2 * (as.numeric(logLik(full_mod_supp)) - sum(mrot_lme_data$log_rt)) +
  2 * attr(logLik(full_mod_supp), "df")
aic_gap <- round(AIC(m_raw_supp) - aic_log_on_raw)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scale-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Angle slope under the two response-time scales, from the same model specification. The log column gives the multiplicative cost (percentage increase in response time per 40° of rotation); the additive column gives the equivalent rate in milliseconds per degree, the unit used in the chronometric literature. Both are average marginal effects over the observed trials."

scale_compare |>
  mutate(predictor = recode(predictor, task = "Overall", item_group = "Item type",
                            site_label = "Site", age_group = "Age group"),
         value = value |>
           str_replace_all(c("^mrot$" = "All trials", "^2d$" = "2D", "^3d$" = "3D",
                             "\\[" = "", "\\]" = "", "\\)" = "", "," = "--"))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("", "Level", "Log scale (% per 40°)", "Additive scale (ms/degree)"),
               booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = c("l", "l", "r", "r"))
```

Two formal comparisons support modelling on the log scale. A Box-Cox analysis, which estimates the power transformation best satisfying the model's distributional assumptions, returns $\lambda$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", bc_lambda)` (95% CI [`r sprintf("%.2f", bc_ci[1])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", bc_ci[2])`]); $\lambda$ = 0 corresponds to the log transform and $\lambda$ = 1 to no transformation, so the interval excludes the untransformed scale. Comparing the two fits by AIC requires a Jacobian correction, since likelihoods computed on different response scales are not otherwise comparable; with that correction the log-scale model is favoured by `r format(aic_gap, big.mark = ",")` AIC units.

These comparisons concern the adequacy of the statistical model rather than the psychological mechanism. They indicate that the log scale is the appropriate one on which to fit and to draw inferences from these data, not that mental rotation proceeds multiplicatively. The two specifications agree on the finding the main text reports, namely that response time increases monotonically with angular disparity; the strictly linear chronometric function is not adjudicated here. Two caveats apply: $\lambda$ was estimated from a fixed-effects simplification of the model, as the Box-Cox routine does not accommodate random effects, and a generalised linear mixed model with a log link would be an alternative to transformation that is not pursued here.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rt-angle_raw
#| fig-cap: "Response time by angle within age groups, with raw per-run medians and 95% confidence intervals."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-align: "center"

# Add raw data underneath
p_mrot_rt_angle_age_2 <- ggplot() +
  # raw per-run medians
  geom_point(
    data = supp_rt_runs,
    aes(x = angle, y = rt_med,
        colour = stimulus),
    size = 0.4,
    alpha = 0.25,
    position = position_jitter(width = 3, height = 0)
  ) +
  # summary CI + lines
  geom_errorbar(
    data = supp_rt_cells,
    aes(x = angle, y = y, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr,
        colour = stimulus, linetype = item_group,
        group = interaction(item_group, stimulus)),
    width = 2,
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = supp_rt_cells,
    aes(x = angle, y = y,
        colour = stimulus,
        group = interaction(item_group, stimulus)),
    size = 1
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = supp_rt_cells,
    aes(x = angle, y = y,
        colour = stimulus, linetype = item_group,
        group = interaction(item_group, stimulus)),
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  facet_grid(site_label ~ age_group) +
  .scale_colour_stimulus() +
  labs(
    x = "Rotation angle (°)",
    y = "Reaction time (s)",
    colour = "Stimulus",
    linetype = "Item type"
  ) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 40, 80, 120, 160, 200, 240, 280, 320, 360)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_mrot_rt_angle_age_2
```

\clearpage

## Full 0--360° rotation functions

The primary analyses model angular disparity as the shortest path to upright, capped at 180°, on the assumption that children rotate via the shorter available route. A 320° rotation is therefore treated as a 40° disparity. Figure S6 tests that assumption directly by plotting response time across the full 0--360° range.

For the 2D stimuli, which were presented in both rotational directions, response times rise to a peak at 200° and then decline symmetrically, returning to approximately their 40° level by 320°. This is the pattern expected if performance depends on angular disparity rather than on absolute rotation, and it supports the shortest-path recoding.

The 3D stimuli cannot provide the same test. The available Shepard and Metzler [-@shepard1971mental] figures were supplied at only three rotations, all greater than 180°, so 3D items appear only at 240°, 280° and 320° -- the descending limb of the function. The check is therefore restricted to the 2D stimuli.

```{r}
#| label: fig-full-angle
#| fig-cap: "Response time by full rotation angle, before shortest-path recoding. Points are geometric means of participant-level mean log response times; ribbons are 95% confidence intervals. Correct responses only, excluding each run's first trial; adaptive and fixed-form runs are pooled. The y-axis is log-scaled, so a constant multiplicative difference appears as a constant vertical distance. 2D stimuli were presented in both rotational directions and show the expected inverted-U about 180°; the available 3D stimuli were supplied only at rotations greater than 180°, so only the descending limb is observed for them."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5

full_angle_cell <- mrot_rt_trial |>
  filter(correct == 1, trial_number != 1, is.finite(log_rt), !is.na(angle_full)) |>
  summarise(m = mean(log_rt), .by = c(user_id, stimulus, angle_full)) |>
  summarise(n_child = n(), mean_log = mean(m), se = sd(m) / sqrt(n()),
            .by = c(stimulus, angle_full)) |>
  mutate(rt = exp(mean_log), lo = exp(mean_log - 1.96 * se), hi = exp(mean_log + 1.96 * se))

stim_labs <- c(duck = "2D (duck)", rabbit = "2D (rabbit)", shape = "3D")

ggplot(full_angle_cell, aes(angle_full, rt, colour = stimulus,
                            shape = stimulus, linetype = stimulus)) +
  annotate("segment", x = 180, xend = 180, y = 1.9, yend = 9, colour = "grey75",
           linewidth = .35, linetype = "22") +
  annotate("text", x = 180, y = 9.6, label = "180\u00b0", size = 3, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = stimulus), alpha = .14, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .65) +
  geom_point(size = 2.1, fill = "white", stroke = .85) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(2, 3, 4, 6, 8), labels = \(x) paste0(x, "s"),
                limits = c(1.85, 10)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(full_angle_cell$angle_full)),
                     labels = \(x) paste0(x, "\u00b0")) +
  .scale_colour_stimulus(labels = stim_labs) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = stimulus_pal, labels = stim_labs) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(21, 22, 24), labels = stim_labs) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "solid", "22"), labels = stim_labs) +
  labs(x = "Full rotation angle", y = "Response time (log scale)",
       colour = NULL, fill = NULL, shape = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "grey91", linewidth = .3),
        axis.line = element_line(colour = "grey70", linewidth = .3))
```
